question: Which evaluation model correctly describes how Java passes object arguments to methods?

options.text: Lazy pass-by-name where expressions are re-evaluated each time the parameter is accessed.
True pass-by-reference where caller reference variables can be redirected by parameter reassignment.
Strict pass-by-value where the reference pointer itself is copied into the parameter.
Pass-by-copy where the entire object and its fields are automatically cloned onto the stack.

explanation: Java is strictly pass-by-value. When an object is passed to a method, the value being copied and passed is the reference address pointing to that object on the heap. Believing Java has true pass-by-reference contradicts the fact that reassigning the parameter leaves the caller variable unaffected.

question: What does the == operator evaluate when applied between two reference variables pointing to objects?

options.text: It checks whether both reference variables hold the exact same memory address.
It compares the hash code values produced by System.identityHashCode.
It compares the internal field values of the two objects for semantic equivalence.
It invokes the default .equals() implementation dynamically via polymorphic dispatch.

explanation: When used on reference types, == evaluates reference identity, verifying whether both references refer to the exact same object in heap memory. The misconception that == inspects internal object content confuses reference equality with the equals method.

question: When two reference variables first and second alias the exact same object instance, what happens when first modifies an instance field?

options.text: The compiler creates an automatic fork of the instance to preserve immutability.
The change is visible immediately when reading the field through second.
Second continues to display the original value because aliases maintain isolated data copies.
Second throws a ConcurrentModificationException upon the next read operation.

explanation: Aliases are distinct references that point to the same single object in heap memory. Any state mutation made through one reference modifies that shared object, so inspecting it via any other alias immediately reflects the update.

question: What occurs when a method parameter holding an object reference is reassigned using new inside the method body?

options.text: Only the local parameter variable is updated; the caller variable remains unchanged.
The caller variable is redirected to point to the freshly constructed object.
Both the caller variable and all other aliases in scope are wiped to null.
The compiler raises an illegal assignment error unless the parameter is marked volatile.

explanation: Because Java passes references by value, reassigning a parameter variable merely changes which object the local parameter variable points to inside that method scope. It has zero effect on the caller reference variable.

The reassignment data = new int[]{1, 2, 3} rebinds only the local variable data. The caller list remains the original 3-element array with first element 99, printing 99 3.
